title: Cooking on a wood stove
summary: A heating stove's top can serve as a hob with hot and cool zones (the sources here cover wood cookstoves, so check your own stove's manual): move the pot, not the fire, and use pans, trivets, lids and a kettle that stays on. Stews and boiling are easy; bread in a Dutch oven or a box oven is an untested experiment, and a real wood cookstove adds an oven the smoke goes round. The dangers are burns, scalds and grease fires, and firing the stove harder to cook faster, which overfires it.

materials.item: Heavy flat-bottomed pots and pans: cast iron or thick steel
Trivets or a steel grille to lift pots off the hottest spots
Kettle or cast-iron pot of water
Cast-iron Dutch oven with a lid, and a small rack that fits inside
Folding camp oven, or a lidded bare-steel box with a rack (not galvanised)
Thick oven mitts or leather work gloves
Lid that fits the frying pan, kept by the stove for grease fires
Working CO alarm and smoke alarm in the room

steps.text: Check before you cook: the stove is sound, its pipe and chimney are tight, and there is a working smoke alarm, CO alarm and extinguisher near the stove (Drolet Chic-Choc).
steps.warn: Cooking doesn't change the CO rule: a leaking pipe joint or an open door puts smoke and CO in the room (Drolet Part 1).

steps.text: Find the hot and cool zones with a pan of water: where it boils, where it simmers, where it only steams (ESSE Ironheart).
Cook in heavy flat-bottomed pans and pots, never straight on the plate: stove paint isn't food grade (Drolet Chic-Choc).
Open any can before it goes on the stove (Ready.gov food). A sealed can or jar heats under pressure and can burst, so never stand one on the hot plate.
Warm cast iron slowly on a cooler zone first, then move it over the heat (Le Creuset cast iron).
Change the heat by moving the pot: hot zone to boil and fry, edges to simmer, a trivet or grille for gentler still, and a lid to keep the heat in (ESSE Ironheart, CMHC wood heat).
steps.warn: Never fire the stove hard to cook faster. A red-glowing pipe means overfiring: close the air fully, keep the door shut and wait (Drolet Part 1).

steps.text: Keep the door closed while you cook. Load the fire, shut the door, then go back to the pots (Drolet Chic-Choc).
Keep a kettle or pot of water on a trivet at the back for washing and drinks, topped up; take it off if the windows run with condensation (CMHC wood heat, NRCan wood heating).
To try bread in a Dutch oven on the stove (untested: no source covers it, so treat it as an experiment), set the dough on a small rack inside, put the lid on, use a medium zone and check it often.
steps.warn: Never put coals from the firebox on the lid indoors: burning coals in the room make carbon monoxide. Coals on the lid are for outdoors only.

steps.text: To try a box oven (untested: no source covers it on a wood stove), put a folding camp oven or a lidded bare-steel box with a rack on the hot zone, with an oven thermometer inside, and turn the food halfway.
steps.warn: No galvanised metal: its coating vaporises into dangerous gases when hot (NRCan says so of galvanised flue pipe).

steps.text: Keep children about 1 m (3 ft) back, turn handles inward, and never hold a child while you cook (MCH scalds).

If grease catches fire, slide a lid over the pan and leave it on until the pan is cold (Kitchener cooking, Tecumseh cooking). Those sources cover gas and electric stoves, where you switch the burner off; a wood stove top stays hot, so also close the stove's air control (our own adaptation: no source covers a wood stove top).
steps.warn: Never throw water on a grease fire, never move the burning pot, and don't spray an extinguisher into it (Kitchener cooking, Tecumseh cooking).

steps.text: Wipe spills up straight away and keep the stove top dry (ESSE Ironheart). Wash cast iron, dry it and oil it while warm (Lodge camp oven care).
steps.warn: Don't put a hot pan into cold water: it can crack (Le Creuset cast iron).

steps.text: Cool any burn under cool running water for at least 10 minutes, ideally 20; for a child, at least 20 minutes (Parachute burns for the child figure; the burns card for the rest).

notes:
## A heater's top is a hob with zones
The plate is hottest where the fire and the hot gases run right under it and cooler toward the edges. ESSE describes its wood cookstove's hob that way: one side hotter for boiling, the other for simmering (ESSE Ironheart), and Drolet says the top of its cookstove isn't evenly hot (Drolet Chic-Choc). A heating stove's top varies the same way, but every stove differs, so find yours with a pan of water: where it rolls, where it simmers, where it only steams.

Control the heat by moving the pot, not by firing harder:
- **Hot zone:** boiling, frying, searing.
- **Edges and back:** simmering, stews, keeping food warm.
- **On a trivet or steel grille:** gentler still. CMHC puts a kettle on a grille or trivet rather than straight on the stove, which also stops condensation rusting the top as it cools (CMHC wood heat).
- **A lid** keeps the heat in the pot.

Cook in pots and pans, not on the plate itself: stove paint isn't food grade (Drolet Chic-Choc). Drolet recommends heat-resistant steel or aluminium cookware on its cookstove top (Drolet Chic-Choc). Wipe spills up straight away, and dry the plate after, or it rusts (ESSE Ironheart).

## Never fire it hotter to cook faster
Too much air makes very high temperatures that damage the stove and chimney and can start a chimney fire (Drolet Part 1). Drolet's signs of overfiring: a roaring fire, the connector pipe glowing red, and extreme heat coming off the stove. If you see them, don't open the door; close the air control fully and wait until the glow is gone. Even at the start of a load the fire shouldn't burn flat out for more than a few minutes (Drolet Part 1). For speed, use the hot zone, a lid, a pan that fits, and food cut small. See [Install a wood stove](#guides/build_stove_install) for what a red pipe means.

Keep the door shut while you cook. Drolet says to run its cookstove only with the door fully closed: left partly open, gas and flame can be drawn out into the room (Drolet Chic-Choc, Drolet Part 1). The stove is safe to cook on only because its smoke goes up a sound chimney, so the CO alarm stays on and working (see [Cooking indoors in a winter outage](#guides/reference_cooking_indoors) and [CO poisoning](#guides/safety_carbon_monoxide)).

## The kettle that stays on
A kettle or cast-iron pot of water on the stove gives hot water for washing and drinks and adds moisture to dry winter air (NRCan wood heating, CMHC wood heat). Stand it on a trivet (CMHC wood heat) and keep it topped up. Not every house needs the moisture: if the windows run with condensation, take it off (NRCan wood heating), and see [Condensation and damp](#guides/reference_condensation).

## Cast iron
- Warm it up slowly on low to medium heat, a cooler zone first (Le Creuset cast iron).
- Never put a hot pan into cold water: the sudden change can crack or warp it (Le Creuset cast iron).
- Wash, dry, and rub with a thin coat of oil while it's still warm (Lodge camp oven care).
- Cast-iron handles get hot. Use thick dry mitts or leather gloves; Drolet says gloves may be needed just to run its stoves (Drolet Part 1).

## Baking without an oven
**Dutch oven.** Lodge bakes in its camp Dutch ovens with three times as many coals on the lid as underneath; for roasting it's even, and boiling, stewing and frying need heat from below only (Lodge coals). A stove top gives only bottom heat, so a Dutch oven there is at its best for stews, braises and boiling. For bread, set the dough on a small rack or trivet inside so the bottom doesn't scorch, put the pot on a medium zone with the lid on, and expect a pale top. No source we found covers bread on a stove top, so treat this as a starting point.

Don't shovel coals out of the firebox onto a lid indoors. Coals burning in the room make carbon monoxide; bake with coals on the lid only outdoors (see [CO poisoning](#guides/safety_carbon_monoxide)).

**Box oven on top.** A folding camp oven made to sit over a camp-stove burner, or a lidded steel box with a rack inside, sits on the hot zone and bakes from the plate below. No source we found tests either on a wood heater, so treat it as an experiment: put an oven thermometer inside and expect to turn the food. Use bare steel, not galvanised: NRCan says the coating on galvanised flue pipe vaporises at high temperatures and releases dangerous gases (NRCan wood heating), so we keep it out of an oven box too.

## What a wood cookstove does differently
A wood cookstove is built for cooking on the hob and baking in the oven, and may also have a warming oven and a way to heat wash water (CMHC wood heat). An open reservoir is fine; a water coil or jacket in the firebox with no vent or relief valve can burst as steam (see [Water coils in stoves](#guides/build_stove_water_coil)). What else differs:
- **The oven is heated by the smoke.** A damper or bypass sends the hot gases round the oven on their way to the chimney; open it straight to the chimney when lighting and when the oven isn't needed (Drolet Chic-Choc, ESSE Ironheart). Drolet says to leave its bypass in the chimney position for 20 minutes after lighting (Drolet Chic-Choc).
- **Small fires.** An oven needs only a small, steady fire; a heat surge after each new load warms the oven and hob again (ESSE Ironheart, Drolet Chic-Choc).
- **Oven thermometers mislead.** Drolet's oven runs about 28 °C (50 °F) hotter at the back left than the front right, so turn the dish halfway through; a door-mounted gauge reads low after the door has been open (Drolet Chic-Choc, ESSE Ironheart).
- **Not airtight.** Drolet's cookstove isn't a well-sealed appliance and needs a good draft, or smoke comes out round the hob plates (Drolet Chic-Choc).
- **A poor house heater.** Cookstoves heat a limited area and burn dirtier than modern heating stoves (CMHC wood heat); NRCan says they aren't designed to be a house's only heating (NRCan wood heating).
- **Cook from the side.** Heat through the fire door glass is intense, so Drolet suggests cooking from the side of the stove (Drolet Chic-Choc).

An old cookstove with no certification label gets the large clearances of an unlisted stove: see [Install a wood stove](#guides/build_stove_install) and [Check and fix a found wood stove](#guides/repair_wood_stove).

## Burns, scalds and spills
- A child's skin burns in one second at 68 °C (155 °F), and most scald burns happen to children under four (MCH scalds). Make a kid-free zone of about 1 m (3 ft) round the stove, turn pot handles in, never hold a child while you cook, and keep hot drinks and pots off low tables (MCH scalds).
- Keep clothing and furniture away from the stove (Drolet Part 1).
- **Grease fire:** slide a lid over the pan, leave it on until the pan is cold, never throw water on it (Kitchener cooking), never try to move the burning pot, and don't use an extinguisher on it (Tecumseh cooking). On a wood stove you can't switch the burner off; closing the stove's air control is our own adaptation, since no source covers a wood stove top, which stays hot for a long time.
- **Burn:** cool it under cool running water for at least 10 minutes, ideally 20; for a child, at least 20 minutes (Parachute burns gives the child figure; see the [burns card](#browse/hazards/burn)).

Food left to simmer for hours at the back of the stove still needs to be properly hot: see [Food safety](#ref/reference_food_safety/temperature_rules).
